scenes.title: Same three numbers. Two answers.
scenes.description: Choose a format, the size of a = 2^E and a small b. Add a + b − a in two orders and watch each exact sum snap to a representable neighbour.

cues.text: Predict both results first. The exact answer of either order is b.
a + b: the exact sum lies between two stored neighbours spaced 2^(E−p) apart.
Round to the nearest neighbour. An exact tie goes to the even neighbour.
Subtracting a is exact here, so whatever b lost is gone for good.
Now b + c first. Its magnitude sits just below a, where the spacing is half as large.
Adding a back is exact. Compare both orders with b.
Agreement between orders is not correctness: both can lose b.

accessibility.text: A number line study of floating-point addition order. a = 2^E, c = −a, b is 1 to 4, all stored in FP32 (23 fraction bits), FP16 (10) or BF16 (7). Near a the spacing is 2^(E−p); just below a it is 2^(E−1−p). (a+b) rounds to the nearest multiple of 2^(E−p) with ties to even, then subtracting a is exact. b+c rounds on the finer grid, then adding a is exact. FP32 with E=24, b=1 gives (a+b)+c = 0 and a+(b+c) = 1. BF16 with E=24 loses b in both orders: they agree and are both wrong. In FP16, 2^16 and above overflow to infinity and both results are NaN. All values are exact binary rounding of these scalars, not a model of a device's fused or reordered reductions.

scenes.title: One weight. Two paths. Add both.
scenes.description: w is used twice in s = w·w and once more in z = s + w. Step through backward and compare correct accumulation with two buggy rules. The stored weight changes only at the separate update.

children.label: Drag or use arrows to change w

cues.text: Forward: compute s = w·w, then z = s + w. The gradient buffer starts at zero.
Seed the scalar loss with bar(z) = 1.
Addition passes bar(z) to both inputs: bar(s) = 1 and a direct contribution of 1 to bar(w).
Multiplication: slot A receives bar(s) times the other factor, w. Add it.
Slot B is the same w. Add its contribution too. Compare bar(w) with 2w + 1.
Only now does the optimizer write w ← w − η·bar(w). Backward left w unchanged.

accessibility.text: Reverse-mode trace for s = w·w and z = s + w with z as the loss. Seed bar(z) = 1. The addition gives bar(s) = 1 and adds 1 to bar(w). The multiplication adds bar(s)·w for each of its two operand slots, both of which are w, so bar(w) = 1 + w + w = 2w + 1 (7 at w = 3). An overwrite rule keeps only the last contribution (3 at w = 3); updating only one slot gives 1 + w (4 at w = 3). A single value of w can coincide with 2w+1 by accident (w = −1 for overwrite, w = 0 for one slot), so test more than one w. The stored weight stays at w throughout forward and backward and changes once, at 5.2 seconds, to w − η·bar(w).

scenes.title: Same gradient. Different memory.
scenes.description: Run two optimizer steps from w = 1 with gradients 2 and then g. Switch optimizer, drop the state between steps, and count bytes for weights, gradients and moments.

cues.text: Start at w = 1 with empty optimizer state. Predict w after each step.
Step 1 with g = 2. Momentum stores m = 2; AdamW stores m = 0.2, v = 0.04 and t = 1.
Between steps the state must be carried. Dropping it changes momentum and AdamW, never SGD.
Step 2 with the chosen g. Compare w2 across optimizers and with dropped state.
The ledger counts payload bytes only: no activations, temporaries or counters.

accessibility.text: Two optimizer steps from w = 1 with η = 0.1, first gradient 2 and second gradient g. SGD: w ← w − 0.1·g, so w1 = 0.8 and w2 = 0.8 − 0.1g. Momentum (μ = 0.9, no dampening): m1 = 2, w1 = 0.8, m2 = 1.8 + g, w2 = 0.8 − 0.1·m2; at g = −1, w2 = 0.72, and dropping the state gives 0.9. AdamW (β1 0.9, β2 0.99, decoupled decay 0.1, ε 1e-8) gives w1 ≈ 0.89; step 2 uses bias corrections 1 − 0.9² and 1 − 0.99² unless the state was dropped, in which case it restarts at t = 1. The ledger counts N·(2·weight bytes + 4·k) where k is 0, 1 or 2 FP32 moment buffers and gradients use the weight dtype: six FP32 parameters under AdamW take 96 bytes; BF16 weights and gradients make that 72, not 48. Payload only; no activations, counters, workspaces or master copies.

scenes.title: Scores in. One target's surprise out.
scenes.description: Move the first logit, pick the target ID and add a common shift. Watch subtract-max softmax, the cross-entropy in nats and the logit gradient p − onehot.

cues.text: Logits are unconstrained scores. The default z0 = ln 2 reproduces the lesson's example.
Subtract the maximum logit. A common shift cancels here, so +1000 cannot overflow.
Exponentiate and normalize. The bars reveal fixed probabilities that sum to one.
Loss = log-sum-exp − z_target, in nats. Greedy accuracy is a separate question.
The gradient is p − onehot(target). Its entries sum to zero.

accessibility.text: Logits z = [z0, 0, 0] plus a common shift. Subtracting the maximum m = max(z0, 0) before exponentiating keeps the computation finite for any shift and does not change p. p_i = exp(z_i − m) / Σ_j exp(z_j − m). The hard-target cross-entropy is ln(e^z0 + 2) − z_target, in nats, independent of the shift. At z0 = ln 2 with target ID 1, p = [0.5, 0.25, 0.25], the loss is ln 4 ≈ 1.386 and greedy picks ID 0, so accuracy is zero while the loss is finite. The gradient with respect to the logits is p − onehot(target): [0.5, −0.75, 0.25] here, summing to zero. Greedy ties go to the lowest ID. z0 moves in steps of ln2/4; the log-sum-exp value is tabulated at those points because the visual expression language has no logarithm, and every other quantity is evaluated live.

scenes.title: The prefix grows. So does the cache.
scenes.description: Set the model and batch shape, then scrub eight decode steps. Each token adds keys and values at every layer; each new query still reads the whole cached prefix.

cues.text: Prefill stores keys and values for every prompt token. Causal prompt scores grow quadratically.
Decode step 1 appends one token. Its query compares with every cached position.
Each step adds the same number of bytes: the cache grows linearly with tokens.
Eight decodes later the per-step attention work is larger than at the start; the cache did not make it constant.

accessibility.text: Dense key/value cache payload = 2 × layers × batch × cached tokens × KV heads × head width × bytes per value, where 2 counts keys and values. Query heads do not enter the formula when they differ from KV heads. Defaults: 3 layers, batch 2, 5 prompt tokens, 2 KV heads, width 4, 2 bytes: 960 bytes after prefill and 192 more bytes per decoded token. Prefill of P prompt tokens computes P(P+1)/2 causal score pairs per head and layer; decode step n has P + n cached tokens and its new query reads all of them. Payload only: no weights, allocator overhead or attention workspace.

scenes.title: Built is not computed.
scenes.description: Build a tiny lazy graph for one gradient step, then choose what to evaluate. Only requested values and their dependencies are materialized; a timer stopped too early measures only part of the step.

children.text: Old L uses old w; it

cues.text: Python lines run and build graph nodes. Shapes are known; no arithmetic has happened yet.
The whole step is declared: residual, loss, gradient and updated weight are all pending.
Evaluation materializes the requested arrays and only what they depend on.
The timer covers only the work it waited for. The costs here are invented.
The next iteration needs w_new. Evaluating the old loss alone does not provide it.

accessibility.text: A lazy graph for one step of L = mean((w·x − y)²)/2 with x = [1, 2], y = [2, 4]. Residual r = [w − 2, 2w − 4]; L = 1.25(w − 2)²; gradient g = 2.5(w − 2); w_new = w − η·g. At w = 1, η = 0.1: L = 1.25, g = −2.5, w_new = 1.25 and the next loss is 0.703125. Building the graph computes nothing. eval(loss) materializes r and L only; g and w_new stay pending, so the next iteration is not ready. eval(loss, grad, w_new) materializes all four. Invented costs (build 0.4, r 0.6, L 0.5, g 1.5, update 0.3 ms) show a timer covering 0.4, 1.5 or 3.3 of the 3.3 ms step. These are not MLX measurements; the order of evaluation is the point.

scenes.title: Finite. Repeatable. Wrong.
scenes.description: A small attention-output analogue: O = P·V. Switch the kernel between a correct row read and a transposed read, edit P, and climb the evidence ladder. Only the reference comparison sees the bug, and only for a non-symmetric P.

cues.text: P holds attention weights (rows sum to one); V holds values. The reference is O = P·V.
Highlighted cells are what the kernel uses for output row 0.
The candidate output is finite and identical on every run.
An independent reference computes P·V directly.
Only elementwise comparison rejects the bug. The backward row scalar D0 = Σ dO·O is damaged too.

accessibility.text: An anonymized two-by-two analogue of a layout defect. P = [[a, 1−a], [b, 1−b]], V = [[2, −1], [4, 3]], reference O = P·V. The buggy kernel reads P transposed. With a = 0.25, b = 0.6 the reference is [[3.5, 2], [2.8, 0.6]] and the candidate is [[2.9, 1.55], [3.1, 0.45]]: finite, repeatable and wrong, with maximum absolute error 0.6. The backward row scalar D0 = dO0 · O0 with dO0 = [1, 2] is 7.5 for the reference and 6 for the candidate. When a + b = 1, P is symmetric, the transpose is invisible and every check passes: choose non-symmetric probes. This illustrates the evidence ladder; it is not a reproduction of any device's lane mapping.

scenes.title: Recompute the same forward.
scenes.description: Trade a retained activation for a replayed multiplication. Then let an optimizer write w2 early: replaying with live weights differentiates a forward that never happened.

cues.text: Forward with w1 = 2 and w2 = 3: h = 2x, y = 3h.
Save h (memory) or free it and plan to replay the multiplication (compute).
Hazard: an optimizer writes a new w2 before backward has run.
Backward: ∂y/∂w1 = w2·x. A correct replay uses the forward-time w2.
Compare with the reference 3x. Equal memory savings, different correctness.

accessibility.text: y = w2·(w1·x) with forward weights w1 = 2, w2 = 3. h = 2x, y = 3h; at x = 4, h = 8 and y = 24. Saving h retains a 1,024-element FP32 buffer (4,096 bytes) and replays nothing; recomputing frees it and replays 1,024 multiplications during backward. Before backward an optimizer writes w2 early (default 5). The reference sensitivity ∂y/∂w1 = 3x = 12 at x = 4. Saving or replaying with saved weights gives 12; replaying with live weights gives 5·4 = 20, a finite and wrong gradient. If the early value equals 3 or x = 0 the bug is invisible, so a test needs a changed weight and non-zero input. ∂y/∂w2 = h is unaffected because w1 did not change.

scenes.title: Same code. A different story.
scenes.description: Four synthetic reference/candidate pairs run in eight slots while the machine drifts slower. Change the run order, the drift and whether a warm-up trial is counted, and see what each summary claims.

cues.text: Every trial is paired: same input, same boundary. Underlying R = [10, 20, 10, 20], C = [9, 18, 9, 18].
Each slot adds the drift to whatever runs in it, like a slowly heating machine.
With all reference trials first, every candidate trial pays more drift than its partner.
Summaries: median of paired ratios and mean paired difference. Compare with the true 10/9 and 1.5 ms.

accessibility.text: Synthetic paired benchmark. Underlying reference times [10, 20, 10, 20] ms and candidate times [9, 18, 9, 18] ms, so every true paired ratio is 10/9 ≈ 1.111 and the true mean difference is 1.5 ms. Eight slots run in sequence; slot k adds drift × k ms. Alternating ABBA order runs R0 C0 C1 R1 R2 C2 C3 R3, which cancels linear drift in the mean paired difference (still 1.5 ms) while the median ratio shifts slightly. Running all reference trials first gives every candidate four extra slots of drift; with drift 1 ms the mean difference becomes −2.5 ms and the candidate looks slower. Counting the candidate's first, warm-up trial adds 30 ms and pulls the mean difference down by 7.5 ms; the median ratio moves less. All numbers are invented to explain the design, not measurements.
